Triggers vs Collisions

Unity physics gives you two ways for two objects to meet, and every interactive thing you build this year is one or the other. Pick wrong and your coin pushes the player around the screen; pick right and the whole game feels invisible — which is the point. This is the complete reference for the physics family: pickups, hazards, hitboxes, ladders.

The one-line rule

A trigger asks "did we overlap?" A collider asks "can we occupy the same space?" — triggers are for events (you entered a region); collisions are for physics (you cannot walk through a wall). Everything else follows from that.

TriggerCollider (non-trigger)
Is Trigger checked?YesNo
Does physics resolve the overlap?No — objects pass throughYes — objects push/stop
Message you receiveOnTriggerEnter2D / Stay2D / Exit2DOnCollisionEnter2D / Stay2D / Exit2D
Handler argumentCollider2D (no contact points)Collision2D (with contact points)
Needs a Rigidbody?At least one object in the pairAt least one object in the pair
Your game uses it forcoins, potions, ladders, hitboxes, promptsground, walls, spikes, enemy contact

Enter, Stay, Exit — the three moments

Every overlap has a lifecycle, and Unity calls one method per moment:

  • Enter fires ONCE, the first frame the shapes overlap
  • Stay fires EVERY frame the overlap continues
  • Exit fires ONCE, the first frame they no longer overlap

The classic bug pair: Enter-only handlers mean "one event per bump" (a coin is collected once — but standing inside a hazard deals damage only once). Stay handlers mean "an event every frame" (a continuous hazard — but a coin collected in Stay would try to collect itself 60 times a second and crash on the second, because Destroy already removed it). The starter's EnemyController uses BOTH: OnCollisionEnter2D and OnCollisionStay2D both call TryDamage, and the damage cooldown (4.4a) is what keeps the per-frame Stay call from draining health at 60 hits per second.

The tag check — the first branch of every handler

A handler fires for EVERY overlapping object — walls, other enemies, the player, your own projectiles. The first line of almost every handler you write this year filters with CompareTag: 

private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)
{
    if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
    {
        if (StatManager.manager != null)
        {
            StatManager.manager.ChangeCoins(1);
        }
        Destroy(other.gameObject);
    }
}

Read the three habits in that shape: filter by tag (what did we touch?), guard the singleton (does the manager exist?), act and clean up (change the number, remove the pickup). The silent-failure trap: a misspelled tag does not throw — the branch simply never matches, and nothing happens. When a trigger "does nothing," check the tag's spelling FIRST, in both places: the object's Tag field and the string in code.

Why pickups are triggers and hazards are colliders

A coin must not shove the player when collected — overlap is an event, not a wall: trigger. A spike is a physical thing you are stopped by or standing on, AND an event when touched — collider, with the damage handler riding on the collision message. The turret's projectile splits the difference: its collider is a trigger (bullets pass through the player's body until they choose to "hit") but it dies on contact with anything tagged appropriately — and the starter's Projectile also destroys itself on the "Ground" tag.

The settings that break everything

  • Is Trigger unchecked when you meant it checked: your pickup becomes a wall. Symptom: the player stops short of the coin instead of collecting it.
  • Rigidbody-less pairs: two static colliders never generate trigger or collision messages — at least one object in any pair needs a Rigidbody2D (the player carries one; enemies too).
  • Layer collisions off: the Physics 2D matrix (Project Settings) can disable interactions between whole LAYERS — if your layer pair is off there, no message ever fires, tags or not. This is the same layer machinery as the ground-check raycast mask (6.2a).
  • Z position / sorting: sorting layers decide what DRAWS in front; physics happens regardless. An object drawn behind a wall still collides with it — visual depth and physical space are separate systems (7.2a).

Where you meet each pattern this year

  • Trigger + tag + singleton: coins and potions (2.1a, 2.3a), the axe (5.1a), the boots (6.4a), the ladder zone (7.3a)
  • Collision + damage + cooldown: spikes (2.2a), enemy contact (4.4a)
  • Trigger hitboxes: your melee swing (8.3a), the boss's shockwave (8.4a)
